newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU ministers struggle on sensitive treaty reforms.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers struggle on sensitive treaty reforms.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers made little headway on Sunday on key reform issues to be finalised at a mid-June Amsterdam summit.
The bloc's 15 members failed to resolve differences on a number of institutional reforms designed to prepare the Union for its eastward enlargement over the next decade.

In an attempt to streamline policy-making to suit a new era in which the bloc could have up to two dozen members, ministers largely agree that the existing 20-seat executive European Commission should be changed.
But there is a sharp divide over the body's new look.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said there had been "heated debate" at a meeting of EU ministers in this Dutch seaside town over how many seats a new Commission should have.
The Commission has itself proposed slimming down to one seat per country, with a maximum of 20 as the EU expands.
France, however, wants to wield the axe further, leaving a sleek, effective 10-seat body, with all members guaranteed a seat on a five-year rotation basis.
"We all agree we need a smaller and more efficient Commission, but the small- and medium-sized countries insist they keep their seats," Kinkel said.
The bloc's smaller nations, such as Ireland and the Scandinavians, are adamant they will not give up their national voice at the Brussels high table.
"All countries must have their own Commissioner," said one Finnish diplomat.

The Dutch EU presidency had summoned ministers to Noordwijk in an attempt to inject fresh energy into the year-old inter-governmental conference (IGC), fearing it had been overshadowed by the run-up to monetary union and by attention given to trouble-spots like Albania.
"The institutional questions are of vital importance for the success of the IGC," said Kinkel. "We need a solution so that enlargement can be possible."
Several ministers also admitted that British elections on May 1 had slowed progress towards wide-ranging treaty reforms at the Amsterdam summit.

There was scope for progress on some issues, but work on key reforms could only be stepped up once the British elections were out of the way, Swedish Foreign Minister Lena Hjelm-Wallen told reporters.
Kinkel, too, said it was inevitable that Britain would not focus on long-term reforms in the middle of a domestic election campaign.
"It is perfectly normal that Britain should show a certain reticence right now," he said.
Ministers were also sidetracked by an internal rift over whether to condemn China over its human rights record.
Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo last week rebuked France for breaking ranks and refusing to back an EU motion against China at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva.
The internal wranglings prompted Denmark to say it would go it alone and table a motion against Beijing in Geneva this week.

"I regret the situation. I find it unfortunate," Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said. "I would have much preferred that the EU this year as in previous years could agree on tabling a resolution on the human rights situation in China."

Ministers, who met two weeks ago in Rome to celebrate the bloc's 40th birthday, will on Monday turn their attention briefly to employment to consider the merits of including a jobs clause in a new treaty.
The Dutch, who insist the talks are making progress, face a tight schedule to broker a revised Maastricht Treaty.

If the IGC review is not completed by June, accession talks with those wanting to join the bloc will be delayed and risk becoming mired in crucial decisions on monetary union and in French and German elections next year.
